items.body: The Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, the Idaho Legislature's powerful budget committee, meets daily during the legislative session. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho revenue exceeded the state’s forecast for the month of August by $37.5 million, marking the second consecutive month in the new fiscal year where revenue beat projections, according to a new state report. Through the first two months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, Idaho’s revenue collections have come in $51.2 million ahead of projections, according to the August edition of the fIscal year 2027 General Fund Budget Monitor. For the month of August, strong individual income tax collections that exceeded the monthly projection by $40.8 million helped push overall revenue collections ahead of forecast. Although it is still very early in the fiscal year, Idaho is projected to end the fiscal year June 30 with a positive ending balance of $657 million if state revenue collections come in as forecasted for the remainder of the fiscal year. That would leave the state with a surplus of more than $500 million compared to the budget state legislators set. Sen. Scott Grow, R-Eagle, makes a comment during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “My reaction was its very promising report, and I’m glad to see the individual income tax is up,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chairman of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. So far, the state budget picture in fiscal year 2027 looks different than a year ago, when Gov. Brad Little and the Idaho Legislature implemented a series of near-across-the-board, permanent budget cuts to pay for a series of federal and state tax cuts and ensure a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Grow said the increased revenue, so far, in fiscal year 2027 is good news, but he isn’t in a rush to spend any additional revenue. Grow said the Idaho Legislature may have additional, unexpected expenses and bills this year related to Medicaid, wildfire suppression, health insurance costs for state employees and the state’s corrections system that may need to be addressed. Idaho’s prisons are full. Corrections agency will request $45.3 million to open 3 new facilities. “The challenge is we always have to project a year and a half out when we are working on budgets during the legislative session, so it’s hard to know what is going to happen, which is why we try to be as conservative as we can,” Grow said. If there is still a surplus at the end of the year, Grow said he would like to discuss restoring some of last year’s transportation budget cuts. “With transportation, we had to cut that (budget) pretty skinny last year,” Grow said. “But with all (population) growth we continue to have in Idaho, hopefully we can get some money for transportation to help with the state highways – not just the maintenance, but to actually help with additional highways we need and expansion.” The Idaho Legislature is not in session, but the 2027 regular legislative session begins Jan. 11 at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. 2026-08-BudgetMonitor GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The South Idaho Correctional Institution sign outside the facility in Kuna. The facility houses about 400 women and 300 men. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was corrected at 9 a.m., Sept. 16 to reflect that women state prison inmates are not sent out of state due to a shortage of beds. They are sent to county jails. If a woman incarcerated at the South Idaho Correctional Institution in Kuna has a dentist appointment, she has to walk through the men’s side of the prison to attend it. To do that, correctional staff must shut down much of the men’s side, restricting everybody’s movement to get her to her appointment. There are nearly 400 women and 300 men at the medium-security prison , which was originally designed for men. South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand is hoping a new women’s facility, slated to open in December 2027, will help solve many of the challenges of trying to house both men and women there. The new women’s prison is one of three new facilities the Idaho Department of Correction, or IDOC, plans to open within the next year. According to a preliminary budget request, the state agency will ask Idaho legislators in January for around $45.3 million to furnish and operate those new facilities to address a statewide shortage of prison beds. The new facilities will add nearly 1,000 new beds in the state prison system. The Legislature approved funding to build the facilities, but those appropriations didn’t include funding to furnish, equip and staff each of them. In 2022, lawmakers approved $112.4 million for a new women’s prison and $37.6 million for improvements to the medical annex at the Idaho State Correctional Institution in Kuna through House Bill 791. In 2024, the Legislature appropriated $10 million for the new facility in Orofino in HB 768. Bree Derrick (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Correction) “If we don’t open them, first of all, as a state we’d have nearly $200 million of investment that’s going to sit empty,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said at an interview at the South Idaho Correctional Institution. “… In terms of the management of the population, we would continue to essentially limp along in the same way we have done, which means probably over-reliance on county jails and on out-of-state contract beds. And then, as it relates to the women, the women will remain here for the foreseeable future.” The state is short about 200 beds for women inmates, which means some are sent to county jails, according to the agency budget request. Idaho’s entire prison population is about 10,000 inmates, according to state data , but the total prison capacity sits at just over 8,200. The agency, along with all other state agencies, submitted its budget request to the governor’s budget staff at the Division of Financial Management earlier this month. In January, Gov. Brad Little will unveil his own state budget proposal, and legislators will decide how to appropriate funds during the 2027 legislative session. IDOC to request $32.9M to open new women’s prison Idaho incarcerates women at the highest rate in the nation, according to the most recent available data from the U.S. Department of Justice. The state began housing women in the Kuna men’s prison in 2012 because the Kuna women’s prison was full. “We struggle to provide them the same types of opportunities that we do for our male population,” Tyvand said. The women at the facility don’t have access to the ballfields on their side and have more limited classroom and work-training space, she said. The women also live in open areas with bunk beds placed close together, including in the area meant to be the least restrictive. Tyvand said the structure isn’t as “incentivized” as it should be. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) As the Idaho Legislature continues to study the state’s health insurance system before reconvening for the 2027 legislative session, the state’s top insurance official recommended having prolonged study of healthcare issues. The suggestion came soon after Dean Cameron, the director of the Idaho Department of Insurance, started speaking to the Legislature’s Health Insurers Working Group . Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron, right. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Insurance) Back when he served in the Legislature — where he served for 25 years — he said that lawmakers had a task force that met throughout the summer studying healthcare issues faced by consumers, businesses and Idahoans. “It might be time to consider dusting that process off,” Cameron said. Then he delved into how the agency regulates health insurers and other insurance companies — and provided a glimpse into some of the common reasons behind complaints, which Cameron urged providers to lodge with his office if they have an issue. “We take our responsibility very seriously,” Cameron said. A significant amount of complaints that the state agency receives against health insurers are related to claims being denied, along with pharmacy benefits and plan cancelations, according to statistics the Department of Insurance shared with the committee. If Idaho insurer met hospital’s pay raise, state employees’ costs would rise, official says According to the state agency’s data, Regence BlueShield of Idaho saw an uptick in complaints that were ultimately resolved by an arbiter — formally called an external reviewer — starting in 2024, soon after the company took over the state’s contract to provide health insurance for state employees and their family members. Cameron told lawmakers that the rise was partly because the company had recently taken over the state contract, and partly because the state had banned covering prescription medication for weight loss in late 2025. Just under a third of the decisions in the 217 complaints Regence faced in 2025 were overturned by external reviewers, according to the Department of Insurance. The state legislative working group was founded after contract negotiations between Portneuf Medical Center in Pocatello and Regence fell through, leading to the hospital to be out of network for the state’s insurer. Last month, the two struck a deal to go back in-network. For the first time, the hospital’s CEO, Nate Carter, addressed the committee Tuesday. Part of the reason this committee was formed, he said, was to navigate through contracting issues — which he said his hospital was glad to have resolved with Regence. “But also this committee is meant for a much larger purpose, which is to assist providers and insurers both in working together to make sure that patients, my neighbors, my friends, and my family have access to high quality care in their respective communities,” Carter said. items.title: We can’t stop Idaho from growing, but with more housing options, we can choose how
items.summary: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down
items.body: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down housing options their communities need. They organize, vote, and pressure local officials to reject more housing. I understand where that instinct comes from. I just don’t think it’s pointing us toward the right answer. Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough. I grew up in Middleton, surrounded by farm fields. Those fields are gone now, replaced by one-acre lots with little infrastructure to support them. I’ve watched Idaho change in ways that make me sad, and I understand the anti-growth mindset. Too often growth here has meant sprawl, distant subdivisions, and longer commutes. But growth itself isn’t the enemy. Communities grow and change, and that change can make a place better, not worse. The Treasure Valley will keep growing. The question is how. During my nearly seven years leading Jesse Tree , the Treasure Valley’s eviction prevention nonprofit, I watched more and more Idahoans lose their footing here. People who worked full time couldn’t make rent, families were evicted, and some ended up homeless. In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening. Meanwhile, most of what gets built on our fringe is the same product: large-lot homes pushing half a million dollars, aimed at out-of-state buyers. Young Idahoans, our workforce, and longtime locals are left out. There’s a better path, and it isn’t new. It’s called missing middle housing, and it’s a return to how Idaho used to build. Missing middle housing means duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, cottage courts, and small-lot homes woven into existing neighborhoods rather than dropped onto the fringe. It’s gentle, incremental density that adds homes without ruining a neighborhood’s character. Look at Idaho’s historic neighborhoods and you’ll find these home types everywhere. This is how our cities grew before exclusionary zoning took hold in the 1970s and made large-lot sprawl the only easy path for developers. It’s also better economics, for residents and for cities. Land is the single largest cost on a developer’s pro forma. When zoning only allows large-lot product, that cost gets baked into every home, which is why half-million-dollar houses keep getting built. Smaller homes on smaller lots bring that cost down and open the door to starter homes again. For cities, more homes per acre means more property value per acre without miles of new pipes, roads, and schools. It’s a better deal for taxpayers on both ends. None of this requires upending the neighborhoods people love. In my experience, when people see what missing middle housing actually is, rather than what they assume it is, most come around. Even hearing opponents soften once they realize it isn’t a five-story apartment complex next door. It’s a duplex that looks like the house beside it. I don’t fault anyone for wanting to protect what they love about this place. I love it too, farm fields and all. But protecting Idaho doesn’t mean freezing it in place, and it certainly doesn’t mean a housing market that only works for people who aren’t from here. It means asking a better question: how do we grow in a way that gives our young people, our workforce, and our own neighbors a shot at homeownership? Missing middle housing is one of the clearest answers we have. If you want to help make the case in your community, Gem State Housing Alliance is activating pro-housing voices across the state, and we’d love to welcome you. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

(Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) One of my earliest memories is sitting behind my dad in his airplane, pressing my face to the window, watching the big buildings shrink to look like Lego sets. I remember thinking: I want to fly a plane one day. The memories of flying with my dad – a fixed wing and helicopter pilot who repaired power lines – stayed with me for years of raising three wonderful children and working in sales. It wasn’t until my early 40s that I completed my private pilot license, the first step in my pilot career. I’m currently completing my instrument rating while working toward my commercial certificate, both needed to achieve my long-term goal of building a career in corporate aviation. My story matters now because women don’t need to wait until mid-life to become pilots. If the calling comes in childhood, follow it. Girls in Aviation Day returns to Boise on Saturday, Sept. 19, and I want as many people as possible, especially girls who may assume a cockpit isn’t for them, to see what’s possible. Women hold only about 5.5% to 6% of U.S. airline pilot jobs. This number has barely moved in decades, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Meanwhile, North American airlines expect to be 30,000 pilots short of what they need by 2032, despite the U.S. government projecting that there will be roughly 18,000 new airline and commercial pilot openings this decade. My timeline was unusual and now I’m training while balancing significant family responsibilities that don’t pause for flight lessons. Training is expensive, and self-funding my dream has meant real sacrifice for myself and my family. I’ve asked myself more than once whether it made sense to keep going. My answer has stayed the same: yes. I credit that to the mentorship I’ve received from other women in aviation. A scholarship through Women in Corporate Aviation last year helped me pass my instrument written exam and keep training toward my checkride. I pay it forward by mentoring girls through our local chapter of Women in Aviation and volunteering with events like Girls in Aviation Day, because I wouldn’t be here without seeing the many women before me who have made it to the rank of captain. Girls in Aviation Day brings around 250 girls ages 8 to 18 to Western Aircraft in Boise for a free day of aircraft tours, hands-on activities, and one-on-one time with women working across aviation and aerospace: pilots, engineers, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers. For many of these girls, it may be the first time they see someone who looks like them doing this job. Representation changes what a kid believes is possible for herself. While I didn’t have many women pilots to point to when I was younger, those in my life are instrumental in keeping me on my career path. I want the girls in the Treasure Valley community to have that now, not decades later. I want women considering aviation later in life, like I did, to know their timeline doesn’t have to look a certain way. Please bring the girls in your life to Western Aircraft at the Boise Airport between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Registration is free at bit.ly/GIAD2026 . items.body: Idaho State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Sean Dolan/EdNews) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 10, 2026. Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.” “I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday. After budget cuts, Idaho plans to maintain low government spending, state official says In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget. All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie. She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose. And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.” However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million. Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation. Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly. Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students. While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it. While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment. This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million. items.body: Wildfire smoke rolls over the skies near Warm Springs along U.S. Highway 26 on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Oregon Department of Transportation) Oregon lawmakers approved nearly $123 million to help cover the costs of this year’s wildfire season, sending money to two state agencies responsible for fighting wildfires. The Oregon Legislature’s Joint Emergency Board agreed to allocate $108 million to the Oregon Department of Forestry and $15 million to the Department of the State Fire Marshal at a morning meeting Thursday. The 20-member board has the authority to allocate funding when the full Legislature isn’t in session. As of late August, wildfires had scorched across 2.5 million acres and cost the state $236.2 million. Those costs are expected to reach $350 million by the end of the wildfire season — putting 2026 on track to surpass the state’s previous $318 million record when wildfires scorched 1.9 million acres in 2024. The forestry department has been able to pay for nearly $79 million of those costs with federal recovery funding, grants and other contributions. With the emergency board’s approval Thursday, the agency will also borrow $150 million from the Oregon State Treasury through three loans over the next three months to maintain solvency through the end of the year. The State Fire Marshal responded to 12 destructive wildfires this year that cost more than $50 million. The agency’s $15 million request will cover funding gaps needed to address those costs. The federal government is expected to reimburse Oregon for some of these costs, though that money can take years to arrive. The Federal Emergency Management Agency still owes Oregon about $92 million in fire management and public assistance grants from 2020. These are grants a state requests if they are facing a catastrophic emergency, and the federal government agrees to pay 75% of the costs. Typically they take about two to three years to be fully released to the states. This is not an unusual amount of money owed, nor is it unusual that it’s taking so long to be reimbursed, according to Joy Krawczyk, a spokesperson for the Oregon Department of Forestry. The slow pace of federal reimbursements frustrated lawmakers. “Through the course of today’s allocations, we’re going to be taking general fund dollars away from our schools, from healthcare, from housing, from public safety, while we’re waiting for reimbursement from the federal government,” said Rep. David Gomberg, D-Otis. Lawmakers on the emergency board thanked all the agencies who worked to put out the wildfires this summer. “It was predicted to be tough,” said Rep. Mark Owens, R-Crane. “We exceeded tough by many levels in that period of time. Without the coordination, the dedication of the state agencies, and I’ll say our Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service, Rangeland Fire Protection Associations, rural fire districts and the volunteers that are out there, there’d have been towns and houses taken out.” Oregon Capital Chronicle senior reporter Alex Baumhardt contributed to this story. This photo is from sometime in 2006. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert) The parking lot was dotted with just a handful of cars on this comfortable August morning. It was the first week of school for many families, so visitors were a bit more sparse than usual. After a two-hour drive from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, to this secluded spot in Somerset County, it was nice to stretch my legs and feel the sun on my face. I had nearly forgotten how windy it can be out here. My brain sort of went on autopilot as my body started to slowly move forward, past the education center and a small group of tourists milling around, and onto a black granite walkway. Every few steps, I’d glance at an engraving in the pathway — marking the time and location of a terrible event that preceded what I’d see when the walkway simply ends. Passing through two towering concrete walls, my eyes were focused on the overlook ahead. The expanse of fields of tall grasses, trees and flowers disappeared from view. I reached the end and stood in front of a waist-high glass window, marked with the phrase: “A common field one day. A field of honor forever.” I was back at the Flight 93 National Memorial. Instinctively, I glanced up at the blue sky. “It would have passed right over my head,” I thought as I looked out at the green field. A boulder marked the approximate area where United Flight 93 met the earth at more than 560 mph on Sept. 11, 2001. Forty innocent passengers and crew as well as four al-Qaida terrorists lost their lives there. It was peaceful now. The sound of birds, crickets and cicadas merged as the wind picked up again. The grass had recently been mowed, and 60-foot-tall hemlock trees still stood around the area that’s come to be known as the “bowl.” Has it really been 25 years since that horrible day? The crash of United Flight 93 is marked by a boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County, on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) The rebellion Perhaps the story of Flight 93 has faded over the last quarter century, so it might be a good time to pause for a refresher. The cross-country flight was headed from Newark, New Jersey, to San Francisco when it was delayed on the runway for about 25 crucial minutes. Takeoff occurred about four minutes before the first jetliner struck the World Trade Center in New York. Once in the sky, the four al-Qaida terrorists took control of the plane somewhere over northeast Ohio. Because of the late takeoff, passengers and crew members were able to gather invaluable information through 37 phone calls to loved ones about the attacks in New York and at the Pentagon outside of Washington, D.C., and what was likely their fate too. So, they came together to try to retake the hijacked jetliner and protect innocent people on the ground. Investigators believe the intended target was the U.S. Capitol, but when faced with the uprising, the terrorists chose to bring the plane down amid the struggle for control of the cockpit. After strikes on the symbols of America’s financial and military strength, al-Qaida designed the fourth blow to destroy the very seat of democracy. Thanks to the actions of 40 people who found courage amid the most terrifying experience of their lives, the terrorists failed in the final act of their attack. (Photo courtesy of the University of Idaho) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 9, 2026. University of Idaho President C. Scott Green will retire on June 30. Green made the announcement during the president’s “state of the university” address Wednesday — an annual event that took a sudden and emotional turn. Addressing the campus community at his alma mater, Green recounted success stories from his seven-year tenure, including advances in enrollment, research and athletics. He also reflected on the challenges of leading the U of I through a global pandemic and in the aftermath of the November 2022 off-campus murders of four students. Flowers and candles left for a makeshift memorial sit near police tape at the site of a quadruple murder of four University of Idaho students on Jan. 3, 2023, in Moscow, Idaho. (Photo by David Ryder/Getty Images) “We truly were at our best when the Vandal family and the Moscow community needed us,” said Green, fighting back tears. “We love you, Scott,” one member of the audience said aloud, before the room rose in a standing ovation. Green’s departure marks a transition at the state’s land-grant university, and sets the stage for another top-tier job search. The State Board of Education — which doubles as the U of I’s Board of Regents — recently filled the president’s vacancy at Boise State University, after a tumultuous and largely closed-door 16-month search. ‘We accomplished more than most thought possible’ A former U of I student body president, Green returned to Moscow in July 2019 , leaving New York City and a top management position with Hogan Lovells, an international law firm. Green said he came back, in part, to bring some stability to the president’s office — a revolving door at the helm of a university established before Idaho’s statehood. During Wednesday’s speech, Green noted that his tenure marks the longest of any U of I president since Richard Gibb. Gibb was president while Green was a U of I undergrad. Green graduated in 1984. Green also discussed several milestones from his presidency. By spring 2020, the U of I had covered $40 million in operating losses , a shortfall inherited by Green. Enrollment rebounded from a pandemic-era lull. Last fall, the U of I welcomed its second-largest freshman class in history . In 2025, the U of I received top-tier R1 research status from the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education , the first Idaho university to reach this threshold. Later that year, the U of I wrapped up a $500 million capital campaign . “We accomplished more than most thought possible,” Green said. On Wednesday, Green also revisited one of his signature initiatives, a failed bid to purchase the University of Phoenix, a massive for-profit online university with a national footprint and tarnished reputation. The State Board gave the Phoenix deal the green light in 2023, after a series of closed-door discussions. The 2024 Legislature balked at the bid — with some lawmakers grumbling that they had been cut out of the process. The U of I and Phoenix broke off negotiations in June 2025 . The requests, which are online on the Division of Financial Management’s website , are for Idaho’s fiscal year 2028, which starts July 1, 2027. After ‘tight budget year,’ Idaho ends fiscal year with positive cash balance On the heels of a 2026 Idaho legislative session marked by budget cuts after years of state tax cuts, the requests outline the state’s strategy of continuing to operate state agencies and public programs with less funding, according to the governor’s budget chief, Lori Wolff. In a media briefing last week, Wolff told reporters that non-discretionary funding for Medicaid, state prisons and public schools is eating up most of a recent projection of increased revenue. “We were very tight on our bottom line before, so it doesn’t give us a whole lot of room,” Wolff told reporters. “That really quickly takes up most of the increase in our revenue,” she said. “So, our focus this year is going to be on keeping those budgets at where we set them last year.” In May, she wrote a memo to state agencies instructing them to only submit barebones budgets, and that the next budget year was not the time to start restoring budget cuts . The budget request for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare — the state’s largest government agency that runs Medicaid and other public assistance programs — is the only budget plan that hasn’t been published yet, the governor’s spokesperson, Emily Callihan, said in a statement. She said officials expect to post the agency’s budget request Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The requests are one of the first major steps in the process to fund state government. In January, Idaho Gov. Brad Little typically releases his own proposed state budget. Then the Idaho Legislature, which meets during the first few months of the calendar year, considers budget requests by state agencies and the governor as lawmakers draft budget bills. In recent years, Idaho’s powerful budget-setting committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, has shifted to a different budgeting process that splits agency budgets into barebones funding and new spending. items.body: A 2023 aerial shot of the Materials and Fuel Complex at the Idaho National Laboratory's desert site. The complex contains several specialized labs where INL researches nuclear fuels. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory) One of the most critical issues facing Idaho is one that has received little attention but has profound consequences for the future of our state – the agreement that would make Idaho the dumping ground for a third of the radioactive waste generated in our country. It’s not surprising that Idahoans don’t know much about this issue. Gov. Brad Little, who is pursuing this agreement , and U.S. Sen. Jim Risch have said precious little or nothing about it, apparently wanting to keep it under the radar until they are safely re-elected in November. New nuclear campus deal would require Idaho to accept, store spent nuclear fuel, radioactive waste Congressman Mike Simpson applauded the agreement , saying it will bring jobs to his eastern Idaho district. “Idaho didn’t become the nation’s nuclear leader by being afraid of hard problems. It became the leader by being the state willing to do the difficult, careful work that others wouldn’t. That’s still the right instinct now,” he wrote. The Trump administration will choose three states to create what it calls a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.” The other states in the running for this dubious honor besides Idaho are Utah, Tennessee, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The chosen states will each have to receive 33 percent of the radioactive waste generated by the other 47 states. The public did not know that Gov. Little agreed to be one of the states until the Department of Energy announced it in late July. The memorandum of understanding that Little signed in July without informing Idahoans said: “The host agreement shall provide for the acceptance of out-of-state used nuclear fuel, spent fuel, and high-level radioactive waste.” In its announcement, the Trump administration promised that the campus will boost manufacturing, create jobs, promote American energy independence, and attract other unnamed financial investments. Of course, we don’t know what this means since Little and our congressional delegation have not told us what’s in the fine print. Idaho’s long history with nuclear waste To put the importance of this issue in perspective, it is important to understand Idaho’s long and dark history with radioactive waste. Starting in the 1940s, the federal energy site in eastern Idaho, which is now called the Idaho National Laboratory, became the repository for much of the nation’s nuclear radioactive waste. The issue came to a head in the late 1970s when the press reported that the federal facility had regularly poured low-level radioactive liquid waste down an injection well above the Snake River Aquifer, which is the size of Lake Erie and provides much of the water for southern Idaho’s farmers and ranchers. There was also concern about other radioactive liquid waste being stored in containers buried above the aquifer. I covered energy issues for t he Idaho Statesman at the time and reported on the controversy over this waste. There was concern among Idaho’s political leaders because the federal site was also known for its porous volcanic soil and seismic activity. Coverage of the issue made front page news for months. That same year the General Accounting Office recommended that Idaho become a permanent repository for the nation’s radioactive waste. items.body: A voter deposits a mail-in ballot at the drop box outside the Chester County Government Center in Pennsylvania on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) Across the country, state election officials are waiting to discover if federal courts will allow the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect. In Idaho, like many other states , election officials are nervous the changes might come too close to the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two months away on Nov. 3. Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic The changes — proposed in a new U.S. Postal Service rule that implements an executive order by President Donald Trump — would require federal review of the design of absentee ballots and impose new rules on the design of envelopes containing absentee ballots, among other things. “In the moment, the biggest concern … is just we’re so close to the election,” Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official and an elected Republican, said in an interview last week. “There’s the practical implications of getting absentee ballots out.” McGrane said he isn’t sure that Idaho or other states would be able to fully comply with the USPS rule if it takes effect before this year’s election. He said county clerks across Idaho, who run the state’s elections, are busy finalizing ballots to print and mail out absentee ballots to military and overseas voters by Sept. 19. In Idaho’s largest county, Ada — which is home to Boise — election officials have told the state they need to know about any changes to ballots by Wednesday in order to make changes before they print the ballots, said Trent Tripple, the Republican elected county clerk for Ada County. He said he also worries about making big changes months before the election. “If you want the most secure election possible, do not put artificial timelines and make us change things at the last second,” he said in an interview. “If you’re doing that, I guarantee you there will be mistakes that are made — because we don’t have the time. We can’t back up an election.” And that’s all on top of other potential ballot changes facing Idaho election officials as the Idaho Supreme Court weighs a lawsuit by the organizers of Proposition 1, an abortion legalization ballot initiative, that challenges state officials’ descriptions of the initiative . (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots. The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho Attorney General and Secretary of State that they must submit revised ballot language to the court by 5 p.m. Saturday — around 24 hours after the decision was entered. Idaho Supreme Court Justice Gregory Moeller, right, asks a question during a hearing in this April 25, 2025, file photo. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The decision, written by Justice Gregory Moeller, found that neither the “yes” or “no” effect statements met the law’s requirements. “A statement is not ‘clear’ if it leaves voters uncertain about a principal legal consequence of their choice, and it does not describe ‘the effect’ of a vote if it materially misstates that consequence,” Moeller wrote. “Conciseness permits Respondents to omit unnecessary detail; it does not permit them to convey an inaccurate picture of the effect of a specific vote.” The ballot “effect statements,” required under state law to be a clear and concise explanation of the impacts of a yes or no vote, were written by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane. The state’s high court heard oral arguments Wednesday and issued a speedy ruling as election officials neared a Sept. 11 deadline to be able to send ballots to military and overseas voters. Supporters of the initiative, called Prop 1, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 27, arguing that the drafted effect statements of “yes” or “no” votes on the ballot measure were “misleading” and “confusing.” Attorneys representing Labrador and McGrane defended the statements in court, arguing they were the clearest and shortest way to inform voters. Joe Parris, a spokesperson for the secretary of state, said Friday the office is working to comply with the order. “We appreciate the Idaho Supreme Court’s prompt review of Proposition One yes-and-no effect statements,” Parris said in an email. “As directed by the court, we are working closely with the Attorney General’s Office to prepare and submit revised statements. items.body: Idaho’s abortion ban applies to any stage of pregnancy, with affirmative defenses for cases of rape and incest with an accompanying police report and if an abortion is necessary to save a patient’s life. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) A panel of judges has placed on hold a federal court order protecting an Idaho fetal medicine doctor from prosecution for abortions performed in specific circumstances. The order means Idaho’s abortion laws are fully in effect, with only exemptions to protect the life of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester if a police report has been filed. Doctors who perform abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties and revocation or suspension of their medical license. Idaho federal judge narrows abortion ruling to only protect Boise doctor who filed lawsuit The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel on Thursday blocked a ruling that would’ve carved out new exemptions in Idaho’s strict abortion ban for the doctor challenging the law. The order will be in place until Ninth Circuit judges are scheduled to hear arguments on Sept. 22. Previously, U.S. District of Idaho Court Judge B. Lynn Winmill wrote in an 81-page decision on Aug. 13 that abortions could be performed in cases where the mother faced serious health risks or risk of self-harm, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. However, after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the ruling, Winmill n arrowed the decision to only protect the doctor who filed the lawsuit challenging Idaho’s abortion ban, Dr. Stacy Seyb. Seyb, represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice, challenged the constitutionality of Idaho abortion ban’s limited exceptions “The Constitution protects pregnant people’s access to life- and health-preserving abortion care,” Lawyering Project Executive Director Stephanie Toti said in an email to the Sun “We are hopeful that the court of appeals will allow that care to resume after it hears oral argument later this month.” Idaho Family Policy Center attorneys file brief in support of law on half of Idaho lawmakers Attorneys with the Idaho Family Policy Center, a conservative Christian lobbying group, filed a brief in support of Idaho’s abortion ban on behalf of 54 Idaho state legislators. Idaho Family Policy Center Legal Director Caleb Pirc wrote that Winmill’s decision went beyond his authority. “The district court improperly made policy for the people of Idaho,” Pirc wrote. “It may have thought its policy was better than the Legislature’s, but that was not its judgment to make.” The brief says that the authority to create abortion policy rests solely with the Legislature. The lawmakers represented by the brief include 37 House representatives and 17 senators, all Republicans, including leaders from both chambers. Those closures affect the Black Rock Campground, Upper Crooked River Trailhead and Lower Crooked River Trailhead, officials said. There were about 600 personnel fighting the Crooked Fire as of Thursday, as well as eight helicopters, 22 engines and 14 pieces of heavy equipment, according to Great Basin Incident Management Team 3. Containment was estimated at 21% as of Thursday. items.body: From left, incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, Democrat David Roth, and independent Todd Achilles. Idaho Democrat David Roth, who had been running for the U.S. Senate seat held by Idaho Republican Jim Risch, officially withdrew his name from the ballot just days before the deadline. Roth submitted his withdrawal form on Aug. 28, citing a “lack of support from Democratic Party,” according to the form obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun in a public records request. A spokesperson for the Idaho Democratic Party declined to comment. Roth faced pressure from fellow Democrats to clear way for independent candidate Roth announced he was ending his campaign on July 28, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. He had faced strong pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles, who argued an independent had a better chance of defeating the longtime incumbent in a head-to-head race. Roth did not endorse Achilles. Roth told the Sun he didn’t want to drop out, but he felt like he didn’t have a choice. He’d also received a letter from leaders of Ada County Democrats asking him to drop out , the Spokesman-Review reported. “Without support from Ada County, I mean that really hindered fundraising or campaign ability,” Roth told the Sun in a phone interview. “And when you have so many people who hold leadership positions in the party advocating for a candidate besides their nominee, it makes it really just impossible.” Roth’s most recent federal election filing shows he garnered about $14,600 in contributions but that his campaign had about $10,100 in debts and loans to be paid back, as of June 30. Roth ran for federal office in 2022 and 2024 and for the state Legislature in 2020. He said this run was “probably the worst experience I’ve ever been through in my entire life.” “And I’ve been through a lot,” he said. He expressed disappointment in his party leaders for not supporting the Democratic nominee in the race after he won his primary contest in May. “It’s an unfortunate situation,” he said. “I think the Democratic voters of Idaho have really lost their opportunity to have a voice, and I think it just goes to show how broken our whole system is.” Achilles’ most recent campaign finance filing shows he’s raised nearly $700,000, although his campaign has recently advertised he’s collected over $1 million. Risch’s warchest was more than $4.4 million as of June 30. The Federal Election Commission requires quarterly reporting on campaign contributions and expenditures, and the next filing deadline is Oct. 15. Without Roth’s formal withdrawal, his name would’ve still appeared on the Nov. 3 general election ballot. Achilles’ campaign has repeatedly said his odds are better if the contest is between him and Risch. “I respect Roth running and making the decision that the campaign just didn’t have the resources it needed to be competitive,” Achilles said in an interview. “I think it’s all about being competitive.” After Roth’s withdrawal, Achilles said his campaign’s plan is to, “keep doing what we’re doing, which is just being out there talking Idahoans and you know working hard on a campaign.” Risch in an interview for an August story told the Sun he was not concerned after Roth announced his departure from the race. “I know people are getting excited all of a sudden because I was running against two Democrats, and now I’m running against one Democrat,” Risch said, referencing that Achilles previously was a Democratic state legislator. “I’ve done that all my life.” Risch, Achilles, independent Natalie Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby will appear on ballots for the U.S. Senate race. items.body: Idaho's state prison system formally entered into an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It's the second state agency to enter the 287(g) program. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s state prison system has entered into a formal agreement with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. It’s the second state agency to join the federal immigration program. The Idaho Department of Correction on Aug. 28 joined the 287(g ) program, which allows local law enforcement to carry out some limited immigration enforcement with supervision from federal authorities, according to ICE records of participating agencies. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Idaho has a responsibility to uphold the rule of law and protect the people of our state,” Gov. Brad Little said in a press release. “This agreement gives Idaho another tool to make sure criminal aliens who are subject to federal immigration enforcement are transferred to federal custody when they have completed their Idaho sentences. Idaho will continue working with the Trump administration to secure our communities and support the enforcement of our nation’s laws.” The state prison agency’s agreement follows what’s called the “warrant service” model, which allows designated officers within the agency to serve warrants to undocumented people in custody. The agreement “formalizes a process IDOC has already been using to assist ICE,” according to a press release from the governor’s office. Correction staff have historically provided ICE with information on inmates with felony convictions to allow the federal agents to identify those who may be subject to immigration detainers, which are requests by ICE to hold individuals to prevent the release of people who may be undocumented, the release said. Bree Derrick (Photo from Idaho Department of Correction) “IDOC has a longstanding responsibility to coordinate with our federal partners when individuals in our custody are subject to federal immigration enforcement,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said in the press release. “This agreement strengthens that coordination and gives our department a clear, formal process for serving ICE warrants and transferring individuals into federal custody when their Idaho sentences are complete.” The state prison agency also “facilitates due process hearings for individuals undergoing deportation proceedings and coordinates with ICE when Idaho sentences are satisfied,” the release said. In June 2025 , Idaho State Police entered a 287(g) agreement with ICE to help transport state inmates to federal detention facilities for deportation. This agreement was funded by the governor’s office emergency funds. As of May, ISP had transported more than 80 people out of correctional facilities, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. An Idaho Capital Sun analysis found some cases where charges were dismissed or still pending when the person was transported to an ICE facility. ISP leaders later said the agency changed its procedure to ensure convictions were secured before transporting individuals. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Months after protestors wouldn’t leave the lobby of the Idaho governor’s office in an attempt to meet with him over anti-transgender bills, a jury on
items.body: An Ada County prosecuting attorney and an Idaho State Police trooper watch body cam footage leading up to the arrest of the Rev. Sara LaWall on trespassing charges at her trial in Boise on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Months after protestors wouldn’t leave the lobby of the Idaho governor’s office in an attempt to meet with him over anti-transgender bills, a jury on Tuesday found a local minister guilty on a misdemeanor trespassing charge. The jury found the Rev. Sara LaWall — who wore a clerical collar under a rainbow speckled blazer as she sat in court — guilty of trespassing after prosecutors said she remained in the governor’s office after being warned it was closed for the night during a protest of anti-trans bills this spring. Idaho’s transgender bathroom ban is now the law. How will police enforce it? That’s still unclear. After the jury delivered the verdict, LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, told reporters that the possible prison sentence she could face would be less time than judges can dole out for violations of Idaho’s new criminal transgender bathroom ban . “That just feels wholly unfair and outsized and ridiculous,” LaWall told reporters after her trial. “… The jury found me guilty of staying in the governor’s office after being told to leave. I didn’t dispute those facts. But someone going to the bathroom now has a higher sentence, and that just feels so disproportionate and so wrong.” Under state law , her trespassing charge is punishable by up to six months in prison. The state’s bathroom ban allows for up to a year in prison on a first offense and up to five years on repeat offenses. Minutes after the nearly full-day trial finished Tuesday, the jury reached its verdict. LaWall will be sentenced on the charge later. Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball scheduled her sentencing for Sept. 17. LaWall’s attorney requested her sentencing be delayed instead of issued Tuesday evening. She hopes at her sentencing she can share more about why she was at the governor’s office. “I have really mixed feelings,” LaWall said of the verdict. “It’s hard not to feel a little emotional about the verdict, but I don’t — I’m not entirely surprised. I took the stand and said as much as the judge allowed me to say about why we were there, which wasn’t very much, and that was disappointing to me to not be able to tell more of the story about why we were there.” LaWall was one of nine protestors who were arrested on trespassing charges at the April 1 protest. At the protest, LaWall and others waited in the lobby in the governor’s office for more than three hours. The protest came a day after Gov. items.body: A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise, as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) Congressman Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho (Photo courtesy of Russ Fulcher’s official website) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher signed on to federal legislation to limit federal law enforcement’s access to data from automated license plate readers, like Flock cameras, and other surveillance equipment. Fulcher announced Monday in a press release that he is co-sponsoring H.R. 9716 , called the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery Act, or Privacy Act. The legislation would, in most cases, require federal law enforcement to obtain a warrant from a federal judge before accessing surveillance data from state and local systems, including cameras that capture images of vehicle occupants, long-range microphones, electronic fingerprint detection technology, and “substantially similar technology” as determined by the U.S. attorney general, according to the press release. “I’m proud to sign on to this legislation to protect the privacy rights of Idahoans from increasingly intrusive surveillance data collection and to prohibit the widespread deployment of such surveillance tools with federal dollars,” Fulcher said in the press release. “It’s simple: if the federal government wants to access state and local systems’ data on citizens, they need to get a warrant.” The legislation would also put time limits on the retention of data federal authorities obtained, unless a court authorizes an extension or the data is needed as evidence for ongoing prosecution. The bill would also prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or install surveillance devices, with some exceptions for systems used solely for toll collections on federally funded highways, school violence prevention programs, grants provided under the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act, and portable systems for specific law enforcement operations with a warrant. The bill, brought by Texas Republican U.S. Rep. Keith Self, was introduced July 15 and has not yet been voted on by a committee. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idahoans have expressed concerns about surveillance cameras A number of Idaho cities statewide have contracts for automated license plate readers, called ALPRs, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Flock is the most common and well-known brand of this type of camera. In July, nearly 100 residents filled the Caldwell City Council chambers, and about a dozen of them spoke about their concern about the city’s use of Flock cameras , the Idaho Press reported. All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state A 2025 Idaho state law prevents these readers from being used for anything other than “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.” However, Twin Falls cameras were searched at least 631 times in March, May and June of 2026 for immigration-related searches, the Sun reported. The searches originated from outside Idaho, and later the Twin Falls Police Department changed its network sharing policies to avoid inadvertently running afoul of Idaho law and its own restrictions on immigration searches. In March, then-Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife’s vehicle hundreds of times between July and September 2025, KMVT reported. Oppedyk retired in April. In early August, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers across the nation had been charged with or accused of misusing the cameras to track women. Fulcher’s office regularly polls constituents who email him, and recent polls found that data privacy was one of their top concerns, Fulcher told the Idaho Capital Sun in an Aug. 12 interview. “The data privacy stuff, especially recently with the Flock cameras, that has got a lot of people on edge,” Fulcher said. items.body: A replica of the Liberty Bell sits outside of the Idaho Statehouse, as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In May 1950, Idaho’s very own version of the Liberty Bell arrived in the Gem State. Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) Nearly a year later, the bell found its home: Sitting prominently in front of grand steps leading up to the Idaho State Capitol — and being loudly rung by passersby. But before it was mounted at the state’s Capitol, the bell toured the state on the back of a pickup truck. And as Americans commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday this year, Idaho’s Liberty Bell is headed back on tour . “We want to have people experience the birth of a nation,” Idaho Treasurer Julie Ellsworth said in an interview. “… We want a memorable thing that touches every place of Idaho.” The tour starts Wednesday with a round of stops in East Idaho, starting in Pocatello and working its way further east, before visiting each of the state’s 44 counties. But how did Idaho even get its own version of the Liberty Bell? The bell — modeled after the cracked original in Philadelphia that has become a national symbol — was one of many cast and given to states in an effort to sell U.S. savings bonds, according to a history of the bell prepared by the Idaho State Historical Society. Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell, moved from its typical home, sits on the back of a Ford F-450 flatbed truck. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Trucking a state artifact This will be one of the few instances — outside of its recent restoration — when Idaho’s Liberty Bell has left its home at the Capitol. State officials designed this tour to mimic the original tour of the bell from 76 years ago. On its journey across Idaho, the state’s Liberty Bell will sit on the rear axle of a flatbed Ford F-450 pickup. The state is leasing the custom truck for free from Kendall Ford, an auto dealer in the Boise area, Ellsworth said. The new truck has a few more bells and whistles than the original truck had — like enhanced suspension and Spudjamin Franklin, one of many “Revolutionary Spuds” that the state treasurer created to celebrate America’s 250th anniversary. But it’s also missing something that the original truck, a custom Ford R-5 flatbed, had: a loudspeaker, which was used to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds, according to Janet Gallimore, the executive director of the Idaho State Historical Society, which cares for the state’s artifacts and helped plan the bell’s recent restoration. The 1950 tour of Idaho’s replica of the Liberty Bell was to promote the sale of U.S. savings bonds. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho State Treasurer’s Office) “I … just love the symbology of the bell and what it means, what it meant for obviously the beginnings of our country and the founding of our country, but what that idea of liberty, justice, self-government means to people today. Because it’s a powerful symbol of those things that make us American,” she said in an interview. On the road, the bell will be encased in a cloth cover. At its stops in each county, it will remain on the bed of the truck for display. When will Idaho’s Liberty Bell be near you? Officials aren’t releasing a daily schedule of where the bell will be in each town at a given time until closer to the dates. But Ellsworth says every child that they see on this tour will get a copy of Spudjamin Franklin’s new graphic novel-styled autobiography, which she wrote. Ellsworth said she’ll try to join the tour as much as she can. “It is so symbolic of everything about liberty,” she said of the bell. “But it’s tangible. It’s touchable. It’s understandable.” On Wednesday, the bell will make its journey from Boise to Pocatello — before beginning a nearly three-week tour across East Idaho. items.body: A ballot drop box in Kitsap County, Washington, pictured Aug. 29, 2026. Washington is one of the eight states that conducts elections entirely by mail. (Photo by Jacob Fischler/States Newsroom) A Massachusetts federal judge on Monday declined the Trump administration’s request to overturn the temporary restraining order she signed last week that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a rule placing new restrictions on mail-in voting. The 14-day order published Aug. 27 was not appealable, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani wrote in a brief order Monday . But even if the order could be appealed, the administration would lose on the merits, Talwani wrote. “It is likely that the USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule and that the Final Rule is substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law,” she wrote. She dismissed the administration’s argument that the temporary restraining order came too close to Election Day as a “cynical interpretation” of the U.S. Supreme Court’s Aug. 24 decision that allowed President Donald Trump’s related executive order to move forward on procedural grounds. The high court found that Trump’s executive order, which directed the Postal Service to create the rule, could not be challenged until the rule itself was in place. It made no determination on the merits of the rule. “A Final Rule has now issued and, contrary to Defendants’ cynical interpretation, the Supreme Court has not endorsed the view that any challenge to the Final Rule is now too late,” Talwani, whom President Barack Obama appointed to the bench, wrote. She added that she disagreed with the USPS argument that the requirements of the rule, which would force states to overhaul their vote-by-mail systems ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections and to gain federal government approval of lists of voters who requested mail ballots, were “modest.” The administration is also fighting Democratic-led states and voting rights groups in the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals over Talwani’s temporary restraining order and in Talwani’s court over a longer pause of the final rule. Several Republican state attorneys general, representing Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas, joined the suit on the federal government’s side. The rule’s challengers say it is an inappropriate incursion of states’ power to administer elections, and would likely disenfranchise people who depend on mail ballots to vote. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, and despite his personal use of the service, that mail voting enables election fraud. The administration has said its rule is needed to ensure that noncitizens do not vote in federal elections, which studies have shown is rare. Trump issued the executive order March 31. States and voting rights groups immediately sued to stop it, but the legal battle heated up last week with the Supreme Court’s procedural decision on its emergency docket. The states and groups challenging the law quickly refiled their lawsuits to reflect that the rule had been published Aug. 21.

items.body: Crews are completing the new Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County. (Photo by Julia Barton/Greater Yellowstone Coalition) Correction: This story was corrected to reflect that highway wildlife underpasses have also been built north of Bonners Ferry. Crews are nearing completion of a new wildlife underpass in southeast Idaho after the public, nonprofit agencies, conservation groups and government agencies pushed for years to protect migrating wildlife herds and drivers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass is expected to be completed this fall along U.S. Highway 30, south of Montpelier in Bear Lake County, public officials and conservationists announced jointly this week. The wildlife crossing features three underpasses, as well as extensive fencing on either side of the project to direct animals like deer to the wildlife crossing. “We were seeing just all kinds of problems there; we were losing at least 100 deer a year,” Idaho Transportation Department public information officer Justin Smith said in an interview Wednesday. “Over 10 years, that is 1,000 animals we know we lost.” Officials also said those collisions cost drivers and taxpayers millions of dollars every year. “Our primary concern is the safety of the traveling public. Whether they are going through a construction zone or whether they are in a wildlife area, we want to keep people safe on our highways, and this is part of that effort,” Smith said. The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass represents a partnership between the Idaho Transportation Department, Idaho Department of Fish and Game, the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the Idaho Conservation League and Bear Lake County, officials said. This map depicts the project area for the Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier. (Map courtesy of Greater Yellowstone Coalition) “Rocky Point shows what’s possible when agencies, conservation and sporting groups and local communities work toward the same goal,” Matt Lucia, Idaho conservation manager at the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, said in a written statement. “(The Greater Yellowstone Coalition) has been part of this project for years — contributing time, energy and funds toward the effort. The next step is making sure the federal funding that made this project possible stays available.” To build the crossing, the Idaho Transportation Department secured a $20.8 million grant from the Federal Highway Administration’s Wildlife Crossing Pilot Program. Funding comes from the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed by Congress and signed into law by former President Joe Biden in 2021. The federal grant was estimated to cover 98% of the construction costs, but the project may come in under budget, allowing the state to return some of the money to the Federal Highway Administration, Smith said. Idaho’s first major highway wildlife crossing was built outside of Boise in 2023 Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US The Rocky Point Wildlife Underpass near Montpelier is one of a handful of wildlife highway crossing in Idaho. In 2023, crews built the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass on Idaho Highway 21 near Lucky Peak, between Boise and Idaho City. The Cervidae overpass features more than one mile of big game fencing to direct the animals to the safe crossing. Fish and Game officials installed a wildlife camera at the crossing to document how it is working. In 2024, state officials posted a time-lapse video showing more than 1,000 deer safely using the Cervidae Peak Wildlife Overpass between Oct. 17, 2024, and Dec. 18, 2024. In the early 2000s, crews also built wildlife underpasses north of Bonners Ferry on U.S. Highway 95 when they widened the highway, the Spokesman-Review reported. Smith said officials with the Idaho Transportation Department are studying other highway corridors with heavy wildlife populations, and the state is open to pursuing other new wildlife crossings as well.

items.body: An advisory group is recommending Idaho use its opioid settlement funds to focus on at-risk populations and communities. (Getty Images) An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds. The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve mental health and substance use issues statewide. The council on Friday finalized its recommendation that opioid settlement funds be prioritized for at-risk populations and communities. A summary highlighting some of the counties facing the highest risk of opioid use disorder included Kootenai, Benewah, Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Clearwater, Boise and Ada counties. The state’s opioid settlement fund was created from a nationwide settlement with opioid manufacturers and may be used for certain, approved prevention or treatment projects. Last year, the Legislature approved spending $6.8 million of opioid settlement funds, according to a memo from the Division of Financial Management. Idaho Behavioral Health Council asks lawmakers to prioritize rural communities with opioid funding The council voted on its top priorities at a meeting in June, which included funding proposed for projects that focus on prevention for high-risk populations, behavioral health support for first responders, and developing the behavioral health workforce. Council members on Friday agreed to send a one-page summary outlining risk factors for opioid use disorder and highlighting which counties were most at-risk, using a 2024 report titled the Opioid-Related Overdose Vulnerability in Idaho: An Epidemiological Assessment. “This handout identifies risk factors for opioid use disorder and puts them in the context of Idaho, where those places are, where we may have more vulnerable folks, where we have had higher levels of overdose, where we have high levels of opioid prescriptions being written,” said Sara Omundson, administrative director of state courts and co-chair of the Behavioral Health Council. “All of this is based on research that was done over the last few years.” The council also agreed to ask the governor and state legislative budget writers to prioritize projects that serve rural communities in the state. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE What areas are at high risk for opioid use? Factors that may lead to certain populations to be at higher risk of misusing opioids include lower educational attainment, according to the risk factor summary the council included with its recommendations. Those without college experience are almost twice as likely to misuse opioids, the summary said. The summary also identified other Idaho counties at-risk because of factors such as high prescription rates and high narcotic arrests using data from the American Community Survey , the Idaho Prescription Drug Monitoring Program , and the Idaho State Police Statistical Analysis Center. The top counties at risk based on low average educational attainment are Shoshone, Lincoln, Minidoka, Owyhee, Adams, Benewah, Payette, Gooding, Jerome and Clark counties. The top counties for high opioid prescription rates are Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Butte, Lewis, Shoshone, Benewah, Caribou, Gem and Lemhi. Brooke Green represents Idaho’s Legislative District 18 in the House.
